h1: Working for a brewing equipment supplier as a sales engineer
title: Brewing Equipment Sales Engineer Careers | Craft Beer School
desc: What a sales engineer at a brewing equipment supplier does, the skills it needs and how a brewer or engineer moves into the role in India.
teaser: You get to see the inside of more breweries in a year than most brewers do in a decade. The catch is that you have to understand all of them.
standfirst: Equipment suppliers need people who can talk to a brewer about mash efficiency and to an owner about payback in the same meeting. That is the sales engineer. Here is what the work involves and how to get into it.
sections:
A sales engineer at a brewing equipment supplier sells brewhouses, fermenters, bright tanks, glycol systems, CIP sets, kegging machines and canning lines. Unlike a pure salesperson, the sales engineer is expected to design the solution: how big the brewhouse should be, how many tanks the planned volume needs and how the utilities will be supplied.

Some suppliers build equipment in India. Others are agents or distributors for European or Chinese manufacturers. The job looks different in each case, but the core is the same: turn a customer's vague plan into a quotation that will actually work once installed.
A typical project from first call to handover

It usually starts with an enquiry from someone planning a brewpub. They want a 500 litre brewhouse because they saw one somewhere. The sales engineer asks the questions that matter: expected sales per month, how many beer styles, lager or ale, available floor area and ceiling height, power supply and water source.

From those answers comes a sizing calculation. If the brewpub expects to sell 6,000 litres a month and lagers take four weeks in tank, the number of fermenters follows from that, not from the brochure. Then come layout drawings, a quotation, negotiation and, if the deal closes, coordination with the installation team. Many sales engineers stay involved through commissioning and the first brews.

The best sales engineers combine three things:

  • Process knowledge. You need to understand mashing, lautering, boiling, fermentation and cooling well enough to spot an unrealistic plan. A customer who wants to brew eight times a day on a single vessel system needs to hear the truth.
  • Engineering basics. Heat transfer, refrigeration load, pump sizing, steam versus electric heating, stainless steel grades and welding quality.
  • Commercial sense. Reading a customer's budget, building a quotation that holds its margin and being honest about lead times.

Communication sits under all of it. Much of the job is explaining technical trade-offs to someone who is spending their savings.

People arrive from several directions. Mechanical and chemical engineers who join suppliers and learn brewing on the job. Brewers who want regular hours and more travel, or who have spent years on the floor and know exactly what goes wrong with poorly designed kit. Food technology graduates who start in projects and move into sales.

A brewer who becomes a sales engineer brings credibility. When you can tell a customer why their planned cold liquor tank is too small because you have run out of cold water mid knockout yourself, they listen.

Travel is heavy. Breweries open in Bengaluru, Pune, Gurugram, Goa and increasingly in smaller cities. Site visits do not happen by video call. Sales targets add pressure. Projects can also stall for months when a customer's licence or funding is delayed. You will also be the first person called when something goes wrong after installation, even if it is not your fault.

Pay structures often include an incentive component tied to orders. Ask how it works before you join. Ask too how long the typical sales cycle is, because a long cycle changes how that incentive feels.
The questions that separate good quotes from bad ones

Every supplier can draw a shiny brewhouse. The sales engineer earns trust by asking about the parts customers forget. Where will the hot liquor come from? How big does the tank need to be for back-to-back brews? Is the glycol chiller sized for Indian summer ambient temperatures of 40 °C and more, or for a brochure figure set in a cooler climate? Is there a drain with enough fall under the brewhouse? Can the floor take the weight of full fermenters?

A sales engineer who raises these points before the order is signed saves the customer money and saves the supplier a difficult commissioning. Over time that reputation brings referrals, which in a small industry matter more than any advertisement.

If you are coming from engineering, learn the brewing process properly so you can hold a conversation with a head brewer. Our brewery equipment buying guide shows the questions customers are working through. If you are coming from brewing, brush up on sizing, utilities and the commercial side.

Either way, the gap most candidates have is a structured understanding of the whole brewing process, start to finish, with the numbers that connect each step. That is exactly what interviewers probe.
faqs: Do I need to be a brewer to become a brewing equipment sales engineer?
No, many come from mechanical or chemical engineering. You do need to learn the brewing process well, because customers expect you to understand how they will use the equipment.
Is it a sales job or an engineering job?
Both. You design and size the solution, then sell it and often support it through installation and commissioning.
An engineering or food technology degree is common. A brewing course or certification helps you speak the customer's language and understand their process.
